lesson.title: Same shape, new size

lead.text: Two shapes are similar when one is a scaled copy of the other. Their angles match, and each length is the matching original length times one number.
That number is the scale factor. Matching lengths, such as height with height, are called corresponding. To find the factor, divide a copy's length by the matching original length.

steps.headline: A similar shape is an enlargement or reduction: every length is multiplied by the same scale factor.

lead.text: A designer wants a bigger copy of a rectangle that keeps its shape exactly. She is choosing what to do to the sides.

reveal.text: One factor on every side keeps the shape. You chose multiplying every length, not changing one length or adding the same amount.

steps.headline: A rectangle 2 units wide and 3 units tall is enlarged by scale factor 4. Find the new width and height.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the width by the factor.
Multiply the height by the same factor.

steps.headline: The same rectangle, 2 units wide and 3 units tall, is enlarged by scale factor 3. Find the new width and height.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the width by the factor.
Multiply the height by the same factor.

lead.text: This time the factor isn't given. Match a side of the new triangle with its corresponding side in the old one.

reveal.text: You found the factor from the shortest sides, then used it on the longest. One factor, every side.

lead.text: A photograph is printed small enough for a wallet. Each length shrinks by the same factor.

lesson.orientation: Match corresponding lengths and apply one scale factor to every dimension.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A photo is 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall. It is enlarged so that it is 8 cm wide.

intro.promise: By the end you'll scale a shape up or down with one factor and find the factor from matching sides.

recap.keyIdea: Similar shapes have the same angles, and every length is multiplied by the same scale factor.

blocks.text: You found that a 4 by 3 photo enlarged to 8 wide stands 6 cm tall.
You also found a longest side of 15 cm from a shortest side of 9 cm, and 2.5 for a width of 5 halved.

recap.nextHook: Lengths scale by the factor. Does the area scale the same way?

questions.prompt: A rectangle 2 units wide is enlarged by scale factor 3. What is the new width?
hints: A scale factor multiplies a length.
Apply it to the corresponding width.
Calculate 2 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 6. The scale factor multiplies the width: 2 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3 to the width. A scale factor multiplies.

questions.prompt: The same rectangle's original height is 3 units. What is its new height?
hints: The height uses the same multiplier as the width.
Multiply the original height by the scale factor.
Calculate 3 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every length uses the same factor: 3 × 3 = 9 units.

questions.onCorrect: 9. The height uses the same factor: 3 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 is the new width. The height needs the same factor applied to its own length.

questions.prompt: Which change guarantees a similar copy of a rectangle?
hints: Similarity uses a common ratio, not a common added amount.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiplying every length by the same positive factor preserves angles and proportions.

choices.label: Add 2 units to its width and height

questions.onCorrect: Doubling every side keeps the shape. Multiplying all lengths by one factor makes a similar copy.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling only the width stretches the rectangle sideways, changing its shape.
Adding is not multiplying. Adding 2 to a 2 by 4 rectangle gives 4 by 6, a different shape.

questions.prompt: A 5-unit width is reduced by scale factor 0.5. What is the new width?
hints: A factor below one makes a smaller copy.
Multiplying by one-half halves the width.
Split the original width into two equal lengths.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5. A factor below 1 shrinks every length: 5 × 0.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the width. A factor below one makes a smaller copy.
That takes 0.5 away. A scale factor multiplies.

questions.prompt: On a scale drawing, 1 cm represents 200 cm. A wall is drawn 3 cm long. Find its real length in metres.
hints: First use the drawing-to-real scale factor.
Then convert centimetres to metres.
Calculate (3 × 200)/100.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in centimetres. The question asks for metres.
That divides by 100 twice. Convert 600 cm to metres once.

questions.prompt: Two rectangles have equal areas. What can you say about whether they are similar?
hints: Area gives a product, not the ratio of dimensions.

acceptedIdeas: Area alone does not determine whether they are similar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Different width-to-height ratios can produce the same area. Similarity requires matching proportions.

choices.label: Area alone does not determine whether they are similar

questions.onCorrect: Equal areas do not make shapes similar. Similar shapes share angles and a ratio of lengths.

misconceptions.feedback: Rectangles 2 by 6 and 3 by 4 have equal areas but different shapes.
Rectangles 2 by 6 and 3 by 4 have equal areas and different widths.

questions.prompt: How tall should the enlargement be, in centimetres, so the photo isn't stretched?
hints: The width went from 4 cm to 8 cm. How many times bigger is that?
To keep the shape, the height must grow by the same number of times.
Double the 3 cm.
questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. The width doubled, so the height doubles too. Multiplying keeps the shape.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 4 to the height. Adding stretches the photo. The width doubled, so something else must double.
That leaves the height alone, so the photo is stretched sideways.

questions.prompt: Why does the height use the same factor as the width?
hints: What happens to the shape if only the width grows?

acceptedIdeas: Every length in a similar shape is multiplied by the same factor.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every length in a similar shape is multiplied by the same factor.

choices.label: Every length in a similar shape is multiplied by the same factor.
Because height is always bigger than width.
Each side needs its own factor.

questions.onCorrect: Similar shapes use one factor for every length. A different factor would change the shape.

misconceptions.feedback: Either can be bigger. The point is that one factor is shared.
Different factors would stretch the shape out of proportion.

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. A similar triangle has a shortest side of 9 cm. Find its longest side, in centimetres.
hints: Match the shortest sides. How many times longer is 9 than 3?
Use that same factor on the longest side.
Multiply 5 by the factor.
questions.onCorrect: 15 cm. Find the factor from one matching pair, then apply it to the other side.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 6 to the longest side. Similar shapes multiply every side by one factor.
That multiplies by 9. Find the factor from the shortest sides first, then use it.

questions.prompt: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle is enlarged by scale factor 1.5. What is the new width, in centimetres?
hints: The width is 6 cm. A scale factor multiplies it.
Multiply 6 by 1.5.
Half of 6 is 3. Add that to 6.
questions.onCorrect: 9 cm. Multiply the width by the scale factor: 6 × 1.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1.5 to the width. A scale factor multiplies.
6 cm is the original width. Apply the factor.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is enlarged so its width grows from 4 cm to 12 cm. Its original height was 7 cm. What is the new height, in centimetres?
hints: How many times bigger is the new width than the old?
Use that same factor on the height.
Multiply 7 by the factor.
questions.onCorrect: 21 cm. The factor is 12 ÷ 4 = 3, and the height uses it too.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 8 to the height. Similar shapes multiply every length by one factor.
12 cm is the new width. Find the new height.

citations.claim: New length divided by original length gives 14/4 = 3.5.
